questions.q: In the nonparametric bootstrap, how is each bootstrap resample generated from an original sample of size n?
options: By drawing n observations without replacement, i.e. a random permutation of the data
By drawing n observations with replacement from the original sample
By splitting the data into two halves
By adding random normal noise to every observation
questions.explain: A bootstrap resample draws n observations WITH replacement from the original n observations, so some original points appear multiple times and others not at all — this is what distinguishes it from a simple permutation.

questions.q: How is a 95% percentile bootstrap confidence interval for a statistic T constructed?
options: By taking the mean of T plus or minus 1.96 standard errors
By taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution of T*
By taking the minimum and maximum of all the bootstrap resamples' raw data
By running a t-test on the original sample
questions.explain: The percentile method takes the empirical 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles directly from the distribution of bootstrapped statistic values (T*₁, ..., T*_B) — no normality assumption or formula is required.

questions.q: Why is the bootstrap particularly useful for constructing a confidence interval for a Sharpe ratio?
options: Because the Sharpe ratio is always normally distributed in small samples
Because the Sharpe ratio is a ratio of two correlated quantities whose exact sampling distribution is difficult to derive analytically, and the bootstrap avoids needing that derivation
Because the bootstrap eliminates the need to collect any real data
Because the Sharpe ratio cannot be computed any other way
questions.explain: The Sharpe ratio (mean divided by standard deviation) has a sampling distribution that is hard to derive in closed form, especially for non-normal returns. The bootstrap builds that sampling distribution empirically instead of analytically.

questions.q: What key assumption does the plain (i.i.d.) bootstrap rely on that daily financial returns often violate?
options: That returns have a mean of exactly zero
That observations are independent of each other (no autocorrelation)
That the sample size is at least 10,000
That returns are always positive
questions.explain: The plain bootstrap assumes observations are i.i.d. Financial returns often show autocorrelation (e.g. volatility clustering), which resampling individual points independently destroys — this is exactly the problem the block bootstrap is designed to fix.

questions.q: What does the block bootstrap do differently from the plain bootstrap?
options: It resamples contiguous blocks of consecutive observations (rather than single points) with replacement, preserving short-range time dependence
It uses a smaller sample size than the original data
It requires a known parametric distribution for the data
It only works for normally distributed data
questions.explain: The block bootstrap resamples whole blocks of consecutive observations instead of individual data points, which preserves the local dependence structure (such as autocorrelation) within each block while still producing a full resampled series.
